story: Gates of the Arctic protects the central Brooks Range, the northernmost mountains in the country. Ice-age glaciers carved its broad valleys; rivers braid across their floors; to the south the spruce of the boreal forest thins into tundra, and north of the divide lies the open Arctic slope. In the Arrigetch Peaks, granite spires rise straight from the valleys.

The park is the second largest in the system, and joined to the neighbouring Noatak it forms the largest stretch of contiguous wilderness in the United States. Caribou of the Western Arctic herd pass through on their migrations; grizzly bears, wolves, moose and Dall sheep live here year round, through winters of extreme cold and summers of endless light.

People have lived in the Brooks Range for as long as 12,500 years. The Nunamiut, inland Iñupiat who followed the caribou, settled the village of Anaktuvuk Pass in 1949 and still hunt the land; subsistence use continues in the park by law.

The name is Bob Marshall's. Exploring the North Fork of the Koyukuk River in 1929, the forester called two peaks that framed the valley — Frigid Crags and Boreal Mountain — the gates of the Arctic. The area became a national monument in 1978 and a national park and preserve under the Alaska lands act of 1980.

sightNotes.poi-gates-of-the-arctic-the-gates-of-the: Frigid Crags and Boreal Mountain, the two peaks on the North Fork of the Koyukuk that gave the park its name.
sightNotes.poi-gates-of-the-arctic-arrigetch-peaks: Granite spires and hanging valleys, a goal for experienced backpackers.
sightNotes.poi-gates-of-the-arctic-walker-lake: A long, deep lake in the park's south, reached by floatplane.
sightNotes.poi-gates-of-the-arctic-anaktuvuk-pass: A Nunamiut village in a pass of the Brooks Range, with a ranger station and museum.

entrances: No roads enter the park. Fly from Fairbanks to Bettles, Anaktuvuk Pass or Coldfoot, then by air taxi into the park
Or hike in from the Dalton Highway or from Anaktuvuk Pass
lodging: None in the park; lodges and services in Bettles and Coldfoot
seasonalClosures: Most visits fall between June and early September; weather can hold air taxis for days at any time

chronology.text: Bob Marshall explores the North Fork of the Koyukuk and names the Gates of the Arctic.
Nunamiut families settle at Anaktuvuk Pass.
Gates of the Arctic National Monument is proclaimed.
The Alaska lands act makes it a national park and preserve.

safety: You are entirely on your own here. Carry extra food for weather delays, a means of emergency communication, and the skills to cross rivers and navigate without trails.
Carry bear spray and use bear-resistant food containers.
regulations: Local rural residents may hunt, fish and gather for subsistence, as the Alaska lands act provides.
Leave no trace: pack out everything you carry in.

operatingHours: No closed times or seasons for Gates of the Arctic National Park & Preserve. Visitor Center hours vary greatly by location and season. See Visitor Center Hours for more information!
weather: The climate of Gates of the Arctic National Park & Preserve is generally classified as arctic and sub-arctic, with exceptionally cold winters, relatively mild summers, low annual precipitation, and generally high winds. The weather is influenced by many different systems, and can change rapidly.!!
directions: Gates of the Arctic is a wilderness park, with no roads or trails into the park lands, so visitors must fly or hike into the park. Access begins in Fairbanks, Alaska & there are several small airlines that provide daily flights into the communities of Bettles, Anaktuvuk Pass, and Coldfoot. Most visitors access the park by air taxi or hike in from the Dalton Highway or from the village of Anaktuvuk Pass. River crossings are necessary from both locations.
